## Material confounds

**Confound 1 — reasoning effort bundled with model identity.** Step 3 gives Grok 4.6 and Astra "high reasoning" while Grok 4.3 keeps its current default. Any observed delta is (model weights) × (reasoning budget) × (possibly cost), not model weights alone. If Grok 4.6 wins, you cannot tell whether Grok 4.3 at high reasoning would have matched it. This should be flagged explicitly in reporting, and ideally you'd want a cheap Grok-4.3-high-reasoning cell — but given the $150 cap, at minimum state this confound in the writeup rather than letting a win read as "4.6 > 4.3."

**Confound 2 — calibration exposure.** These 12 papers were already opened, audited, and in some cases used to derive the very failure taxonomy in the ceiling assessment (RYR2 18929323, SCN5A 25163546, SCN5A 20129283 all appear by name there). The plan correctly labels this "calibration, not blinded sampling" — keep that framing in the final report's headline, not just buried in methods. Any percentage from this panel is a diagnostic signal, not a corpus estimate, and should never be quoted without that caveat attached.

**Confound 3 — deterministic short-circuit heterogeneity.** Step 3 notes some papers reach the primary model only via deterministic shortcuts that bypass reasoning entirely. If different models trigger the shortcut at different rates (unlikely if source/logic is fixed, but worth a one-line check), a model "improvement" could really be a routing artifact. Record per-paper which path was taken.

**Confound 4 — Astra-as-independent-reader vs. Astra-as-primary conflates two different questions in one budget.** Step 3 tests "Astra as primary" (a current-production comparison — same pipeline stage, swapped model) while Step 4 tests "Astra as independent completeness check on Grok 4.6 misses" (a direct-reader assay — a different architectural role, bounded scope, no gold/no Grok answers shown). These must be reported as separate rows, not pooled into one "Astra helps" conclusion. A gain in Step 4 says nothing about whether Astra-as-primary (Step 3) is worth adopting, and vice versa.

## Minimal useful contrasts

Given $150, the informative comparisons are: (a) Grok 4.3 vs Grok 4.6 as primary, same workflow — isolates model-swap value, confounded by reasoning as above; (b) Grok 4.6 primary vs Grok 4.6 primary + bounded Astra completeness pass on incomplete results — isolates whether a second independent read recovers omissions without corrupting accepted fields. (b) is the more decision-relevant contrast for your stated question ("can an independent reader improve omission capture while preserving ownership") and should get priority if money runs short — cut Step 5's second-panel extension before cutting Step 4.

## Counting safeguards

The plan already bans "accept a count because two models agree" — good, keep it. Add: track *rejected* Astra proposals, not just accepted ones, so agreement-that-turned-out-wrong is visible, not silently dropped. Also track cases where Astra's independent read *disagrees* with an already-accepted Grok field — the plan says Astra doesn't see Grok's answers, but doesn't say what happens if Astra's blind read contradicts an accepted value. That path needs a rule now, before results arrive, or it will be resolved ad hoc under sunk-cost pressure.

## Budget failure modes

Reasoning-heavy calls (Grok 4.6, Astra) on 12 papers with unresolved counts are the likely overrun vector — "high reasoning" requests can multiply token cost non-linearly on long clinical tables. The $15 retry reserve is thin if even 2–3 papers require multiple passes. Recommend checking actual usage after Step 3 completes on 2–3 papers before committing the remaining 9, rather than dispatching all 12 at once.

## What would justify a wider run

Not: any single-model win on this panel, and not agreement-based count acceptance. Justification requires: (1) Step 4's independent-read gain survives the "not one big row" check (cf. the H558R lesson — 408/511 units from one row), (2) the gain is attributable to genuine omission recovery with source support, not reasoning-budget alone, and (3) cost-per-additional-correct-count is reported and reasonable. A wide run on an unopened, never-inspected panel is the only way to convert this calibration into evidence; this panel alone cannot authorize it.

## Ownership question

Astra's independent read in Step 4, as scoped (no gold, no Grok answer, bounded trigger, raw-vs-accepted separation), is structurally sound for improving omission capture without seizing cohort/endpoint authorship — the design keeps Grok's accepted fields as the default and Astra as a challenger on incomplete fields only. The risk isn't the design, it's discipline in Step 5: don't let a good Step 4 result quietly promote Astra to primary-reader status without a separate Step 3-style comparison.
